# Statewide Universal School Meals Policies and Food Insecurity: Difference-in-Differences Analysis

**Authors:** Kelsey L. Kinderknecht; Eric B. Rimm; S. Bryn Austin; Shoba Ramanadhan; Matthew M. Lee; Erica L. Kenney

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts; | 2Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts; | 3Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts; | 4Division of Adolescent and Young Adult Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts; | 5Taubman Center for State and Local Government, Harvard Kennedy School of Government, Cambridge, Massachusetts

## Abstract

The National School Lunch and Breakfast Program, a US program that addresses food insecurity, requires children with higher household incomes to pay for meals. It is unclear whether universal school meals (USM) policies, which make all meals free, further alleviate food insecurity, particularly for students who would otherwise pay. This study estimates the association between statewide USM policies and food insecurity.

A difference-in-differences study using a nationally representative sample of US households with 6- to 17-year-old children from 2012 to 2021 and 2023 to 2024. The exposure was maintaining statewide USM policy after 2022, determined based on state of residence. The primary outcome was household food insecurity; the secondary outcome was child food insecurity. Analyses were stratified by household income.

The sample included 75 122 households. Households with the highest incomes in USM-maintaining states experienced a 1.3-percentage-point (95% CI: −2.1, −0.5) differential decrease in household food insecurity and a 0.9-percentage-point (95% CI: −1.4, −0.5) differential decrease in child food insecurity. Households with low-middle income in USM-maintaining states experienced a 3.2-percentage-point (95% CI: −6.1, −0.3) differential decrease in household food insecurity but no differential change in child food insecurity. Households with lowest income in USM-maintaining states experienced no differential change in household food insecurity and a 3.8-percentage-point (95% CI: −6.2, −1.5) decrease in child food insecurity, although caution is required because the parallel trends assumption was violated.

Implementing statewide USM policies could contribute to decreased food insecurity among households with school-aged children.

## INTRODUCTION

Food insecurity, defined as limited or uncertain access to adequate food due to a lack of money or resources, increases children’s risk for impaired growth trajectories, poor diet quality, asthma, depressive symptoms, impaired social and emotional skills, worse academic performance, and lifelong consequences related to cardiometabolic health.1,2 One of the largest programs to address food insecurity for youth in the United States is the federal National School Lunch and Breakfast Program (NSLBP), which provides nutritionally balanced meals to approximately 30 million US children.3 Participation in NSLBP improves food security, academic performance, and nutritional outcomes for children.4–7

NSLBP operates by reimbursing schools for serving breakfasts and lunches that meet nutrition standards and other requirements.3 Importantly, these reimbursements are tiered based on the household income of each participating student, which also determines whether and how much students pay for their meals. Students with household incomes greater than 185% of the federal poverty level (FPL) pay full price, and schools are reimbursed the least for these meals; students with household incomes greater than 130% and less than or equal to 185% FPL pay a reduced price, and schools are reimbursed slightly more; and students with household incomes less than or equal to 130% FPL pay nothing, and schools are reimbursed the most for these students.

Underutilization of NSLBP limits its reach and impact, however.8 The paperwork that school staff and families must complete to maintain the tiered payment system is one driver of underutilization; children also report experiencing stigma in school cafeterias when receiving free or reduced-price meal benefits that discourages participation.9,10 Additionally, some children whose household income is low, but not low enough to receive free meals, thus qualifying them for reduced-price meals, still may not be able to afford to pay at all and thus forego the meals.10,11 Schools, groups of schools, or districts with high proportions of students eligible for free or reduced-price meals can opt to address these challenges by participating in the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), a universal school meals (USM) policy that allows individual schools or districts to be reimbursed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for serving free breakfasts and lunches to all students, regardless of household income.12 However, CEP does not reach schools or districts who decline to apply or who have lower proportions of students with low household incomes, despite the fact that even districts with higher incomes can still have many students in need.

In March 2020, as part of a suite of efforts to offset threats to households’ food access and economic stability due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress authorized the USDA to implement an emergency waiver that allowed for schools to serve meals to all students at no cost, regardless of household income, through the end of the 2021–2022 school year.13 When this emergency waiver expired on June 30, 2022,13 most states returned to the pre-pandemic 3-tiered payment system, with some individual schools or districts returning to CEP. However, several states chose to maintain or readopt their own statewide USM policies.14 Although prior investigations have found that CEP increases meal participation and school attendance and decreases suspension rates and child food insufficiency at a school or district level,15,16 it is unclear how statewide USM policies—which can reach many more children, particularly those living in schools or districts that do not qualify for CEP—may impact children, and there has been no research to evaluate the impact of these USM policies on diet quality and food insecurity specifically. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by assessing whether those living in states maintaining or readopting statewide USM policies after the COVID-19 pandemic had lower probability of household and child food insecurity compared with those living in states that discontinued statewide USM, particularly among children with lower household incomes who would not normally qualify for free meals.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Sample

This quasi-experiment used serial cross-sectional data from households with at least 1 school-aged child (aged 6–17 years) participating in the 2012 through 2021 or 2023 through 2024 waves of the Food Security Supplement (administered in December each year) of the Current Population Survey, a nationally representative annual survey from the US Census Bureau (Supplemental Figure 1).17

### Measures

#### Primary Exposure

The primary exposure was living in a state that maintained or readopted a statewide USM policy after the COVID-19 pandemic, measured by households’ state of residence. From March 2020 through June 2022, all households in all states had adopted the pandemic-related federal emergency waiver for USM.13 Households were considered exposed if they lived in states that then maintained or readopted statewide USM policy after 2022 (adopters in 2022–2023 school year: California, Maine, Massachusetts, Vermont, Nevada; adopters in 2023–2024 school year: Colorado, New Mexico, Minnesota, Michigan)14,18; all other states discontinued statewide USM after 2022 and were considered unexposed (Supplemental Figure 2). Seven states were excluded due to having passed legislation that expanded eligibility of free school meals that was (1) not sustained for the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 school years (Nevada, Connecticut, Maryland), (2) not statewide (New York), or (3) not free for all students (Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio).14

#### Outcome

The primary outcome was household food insecurity, measured using the 18-item US Household Food Security Survey Module19 with a 30 day reference period. Child food insecurity, a more severe form of food insecurity, was our secondary outcome, measured using a subset of questions from the same survey.

Covariates included year, the head of household’s self-reported age (aged 15–34 years, 35–59 years, 60+ years), sex (male and female), highest level of education (≤high school, some college or 2-year degree, ≥4-year degree), ethnicity (Hispanic and non-Hispanic), and race (white, Black, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, or Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Multiracial, according to fixed categories provided by the US Census Bureau).20 Race and ethnicity were included based on previously documented associations with NSLBP participation and food insecurity.1,8 Heads of households also reported household income (continuous), household size, number of children, receipt of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, and metropolitan status.17 The ratio of household income to FPL was determined based on household size, year, and state and categorized as lowest income (≤130% FPL), low-middle income (>130% to ≤200% FPL with 200% FPL as the upper limit due to evidence that those above the reduced-price threshold of 185% FPL being in need of subsidized meals), and highest income (>200% FPL).11

### Statistical Analysis

Survey-weighted sociodemographic characteristics were calculated for pre-exposure (2012–2021) and post-exposure (2023–2024), stratified by exposure status. Survey-weighted proportions of household and child food insecurity were calculated for pre- and post-exposure periods, both overall and stratified by exposure status and income level (Table 1) as well as year (Supplemental Figures 3 and 4). Linear probability models were fit using a difference-in-differences approach to estimate the average change in probability of household food insecurity from pre-exposure (2012–2021) to post-exposure (2023–2024), comparing households living in the USM-maintaining states (exposed) with households living in states that did not extend USM after 2021 (unexposed). Data from 2022 were omitted from the primary analysis due to potential confounding arising from the expiration of the expanded Child Tax Credit (CTC) in December 2021 as well as expiration of emergency SNAP allotments, which have been shown to influence food security21; importantly, these competing events may have differentially affected exposed and unexposed states.22,23 Analyses were stratified by household income levels given expected differences in how USM extension would affect households in different income categories, who would be subject to different fees for school meals without USM. The difference-in-differences model equation is shown in the Supplemental Text.

Models accounted for year and household-level covariates including age, sex, race, ethnicity, highest level of education, number of people in household, income (continuous), receipt of SNAP benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, and metropolitan status of residence to account for possible differences in the distribution of sociodemographic characteristics between exposure groups and to increase statistical precision. To examine whether trends in household and child food insecurity were parallel between exposed and unexposed states before 2022, an event-study model with a difference-in-differences analytic framework estimated the association between a state extending its USM policy after 2022 and the probability of food insecurity, using a series of yearly indicators and their interactions with a binary indicator for whether the household lived in a state that was exposed or not. We evaluated whether the coefficients for the exposure-X-year interaction terms were significantly different from zero for years before 2021, with 2021 as the reference year (Supplemental Figures 5 and 6).24

The models calculated effect estimates that predict the probability of household and child food insecurity. Effect estimates were multiplied by the weighted exposed sample to predict the number of households affected by the change in probability of food insecurity. Design-based variance estimators accounted for the complex survey design, including clustering of households within states. The analysis used a complete case approach, excluding households with missing information on outcome variables (household food insecurity, child food insecurity) or covariates (receipt of SNAP benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, metropolitan status of residence), all of which were less than 5% missing.

Sensitivity analyses assessed whether results were robust to the inclusion of 2022 data, with 3 scenarios: (1) excluding households living in states that did not readopt statewide USM until the 2023–2024 school year, (2) excluding households living in states that were late statewide USM adopters and had expiration of emergency SNAP allotments before 2023, and (3) excluding households living in states that were late statewide USM adopters, had expiration of emergency SNAP allotments before 2023, and were categorized as having low cost of living.22,23

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.0.25 Supplement survey weights and replicate weights accounted for nonresponse and complex sampling for nationally representative estimates. Two-sided alpha was set at 0.05. The institutional review board of a private university determined this to be not human subjects research.

## RESULTS

The analytic sample consisted of 75 122 households with children aged 6 to 17 years in pre-exposure (2012–2021) or post-exposure (2023–2024) survey waves (Table 1). Household sociodemographic characteristics were similar in pre- compared with post-exposure periods. Heads of households living in states that maintained or readopted statewide USM, compared with those in states that did not, were more likely to identify as Hispanic, have household incomes greater than or equal to $150 000, and live in a metropolitan area.

Household food insecurity increased for households with children in all states and across all income groups from pre-exposure (2012–2021) to post-exposure (2023–2024), except for those with low-middle incomes in USM-maintaining states. In states that maintained or readopted statewide USM, the weighted, unadjusted prevalence of household food insecurity changed from pre- to post-exposure from 19.2% to 25.1% for lowest income, 14.7% to 13.2% for low-middle income, and 3.1% to 4.5% for highest income; in USM-discontinuing states, corresponding changes were 19.7% to 24.9% for lowest income, 15.1% to 17.3% for low-middle income, and 3.1% to 5.2% for highest income. Meanwhile, in USM-discontinuing states, the prevalence of weighted, unadjusted child food insecurity changed from pre- to post-exposure from 10.8% to 15.4% for households with lowest incomes and from 8.3% to 8.7% for households with low-middle incomes; in statewide USM-maintaining states, the pattern differed between households with lowest and low-middle incomes (from 10.4% to 11.7% for lowest income and 7.5% to 6.6% for low-middle income households). Child food insecurity remained minimal for those with highest income in all states. Similar patterns were observed for the adjusted marginal predicted probability estimates of household and child food insecurity (Figures 1 and 2).

In difference-in-differences analyses, living in a USM-maintaining state was associated with a 3.2-percentage-point differential decrease in the probability of household food insecurity among households with low-middle income (95% CI: −6.1, −0.3) from pre- to post-exposure compared with those living in USM-discontinuing states. This translates to approximately 2900 fewer households with household food insecurity in USM-maintaining states than what would have been expected without statewide USM. Additionally, maintaining USM policy was associated with a 1.3-percentage-point differential decrease in household food insecurity (95% CI: −2.1, −0.5) among households with highest income. For households with the lowest incomes, there were no significant differences in changes from pre- to post-exposure in household food insecurity by USM status (Table 2).

Meanwhile, for households with the lowest incomes, living in a USM-maintaining state was associated with a 3.8-percentage-point differential decrease in the probability of child food insecurity (95% CI: −6.2, −1.5) from pre- to post-exposure compared with those living in USM-discontinuing states; additionally, it was associated with a 0.9-percentage-point differential decrease in child food insecurity (95% CI: −1.4, −0.5) among households with highest income. For households with low-middle income, there were no significant differences in child food insecurity over time by state USM status (Supplemental Table 1). Supplemental Tables 2 and 3 show crude model estimates.

Regardless of USM status, the adjusted models (Table 2; Supplemental Table 1) suggested some racial and ethnic differences in both household and child food insecurity risk that varied by household income level. Black households had significantly higher risk of both household and child food insecurity compared with white households, but only among the highest-income group; meanwhile, households identifying as American Indian/Alaskan Native, Asian, or Hawaiian/Pacific Islander had lower risk of household food insecurity than white households, but only in the low- and low-middle-income groups. Those identifying as non-Hispanic ethnicity, meanwhile, had higher risk of household and child food insecurity than Hispanic ethnicity households in the lowest-income group, but lower risk in the highest-income group.

Tests of differences in pre-trends in household food insecurity between households living in states that maintained or readopted statewide USM compared with USM-discontinuing states from 2012 to 2020 compared with 2021 found substantial violations in the parallel trends assumption for the lowest-income group in particular (2013, 2014, 2017, 2018, and 2019) with fewer for the other income groups (2020 for low-middle income and 2014, 2016, and 2017 for highest income) (Supplemental Figure 5). Similar patterns were observed for child food insecurity for each income level (Supplemental Figure 6).

### Sensitivity Analyses

In all sensitivity analyses, similar significant associations were found between living in the 5 USM-maintaining states from 2022 to 2025 and risk of child food insecurity as the main analysis, as well as significant associations for household food insecurity for households with lowest and highest incomes; however, associations between living in USM-maintaining states and household food insecurity were no longer significant for households with low-middle incomes (Supplemental Tables 4–9).

## DISCUSSION

In this difference-in-differences analysis using nationally representative data, living in a state that maintained or readopted a statewide USM policy after the expiration of the pandemic-related federal emergency USM waiver was associated with significantly decreased probability of household food insecurity for households with children whose income is low, but too high to receive free meals under NSLBP, averting household food insecurity for more than 2900 households. In addition, maintaining statewide USM policies was also associated with reduced household and child food insecurity for households with the highest incomes.

These results suggest that statewide USM policies may have protected households with children with incomes too high to allow participation in free school meals (and several other safety net programs) from a general trend toward higher food insecurity risk. The observed increases in food insecurity overall are likely attributable to the expiration of pandemic-related policies and waivers for administering various safety net programs (such as pandemic Electronic Benefits Transfer [EBT], expanded CTC, increased allotments of SNAP benefits)—which had often set income-eligibility requirements that allowed for households with low-middle income to participate during the pandemic—combined with inflation and a spike in food prices after the pandemic.26–28

Our results echo a prior study finding that statewide USM policies were associated with child food insufficiency, a more acute measure of food hardship used during the pandemic yet not robustly tested for its validity and reliability.15 There are several plausible mechanisms through which USM policies could alleviate both household and child food insecurity. Serving free school meals reduces food expenditures for households and also makes participation more appealing given the reductions in paperwork and stigma. Prior literature has found that USM policies, such as CEP, have been associated with increased school attendance and school meal participation and decreased household food expenditures.29–31

Schools in USM-discontinuing states can operate a universal free school meals program by opting into CEP at a school or district level. CEP is associated with better health outcomes32,33; however, CEP’s reach remains limited as it can be used only by high-poverty schools and districts that opt into it. Many schools and districts choose not to opt into CEP due to concerns about cost; only schools or districts with an identified student percentage from low-income households above 62.5% receive full reimbursement from the federal government, leaving districts (or states, in USM policy states) to make up the remainder of the meal cost to still offer the meals for free if less of the district or school is low-income.34 Due to these constraints, a statewide USM policy may be a more feasible and effective strategy.

This study is the first analysis to assess the association of state laws that extend USM policies on household and child food insecurity, using nationally representative data and a robust quasi-experimental design with validated measures. There are several limitations, however, and our results should be interpreted with caution. The analysis was conducted with the assumption that all children in the sampled households were attending schools that served NSLBP meals, which could lead to exposure misclassification (eg, a child attends a private school). There is also likely exposure misclassification among children living in USM-discontinuing states, given that districts within those states could still have implemented USM using CEP. Because data beyond 2024 are not available, it is also unknown whether the observed association between statewide USM policies and lower probability of household and child food insecurity will persist. Lastly, difference-in-differences analyses assume that the exposure (maintaining or readopting statewide USM policy) is random and that other policies are not being implemented or deimplemented during the same time period. This assumption was not appropriate for 2022, however, due to the expiration of several pandemic-era assistance programs impacting households differentially in USM-discontinuing vs USM-maintaining states during that year, including the expanded CTC,22 whose expiration may have had larger impacts in states with higher costs of living22,35 (which the USM-maintaining states disproportionately were), and pandemic-related emergency SNAP allotments, which expired at different times for USM-discontinuing and USM-maintaining states.23,36 Indeed, in sensitivity analyses that attempted to include the 2022 data (and excluded later readopting statewide USM states), similar associations were seen between maintaining statewide USM and household and child food insecurity for households with the lowest and highest incomes, but not for households with low-middle incomes (Supplemental Tables 4 and 5), regardless of whether we excluded additional states from the unexposed group (based on timing of expiration of emergency SNAP allotments and low cost of living) in an effort to make them more comparable to the exposure group (Supplemental Tables 6–9). It is unclear whether this may have been due to the remaining competing differential effects of the expanded CTC, whether this is a result of lower power from the exclusion of later readopting statewide USM states, or whether this is because no true association exists. Additionally, when testing the parallel trends assumption, we observed violations of parallel pre-trends, particularly for households with the lowest income with consistently negative pre-exposure event-study coefficients (Supplemental Figures 5 and 6). These violations make the results for households with the lowest income difficult to interpret and attribute to USM maintenance. For households with low-middle income, the 1 violation for household and child food insecurity was in 2020, which could be related to increased COVID-19–related school closures in December 202037 and data suggesting uneven implementation of meal programs (eg, grab-and-go meals, pandemic EBT) when schools are closed.38

## CONCLUSION

Children that are ineligible for free NSLBP meals under NSLBP’s existing 3-tiered payment system were protected from increasing trends in both household and child food insecurity from before 2022 to after if they lived in states that maintained statewide USM beyond 2022. As the number of states considering a statewide USM policy rises,39 this study suggests that implementing statewide USM could help alleviate food insecurity for thousands of children.
